summary:
Farmers in Uzbekistan’s Fergana Valley have grown winter wheat followed by cotton for generations. NASA’s record of that land shows why this is getting harder: 194 mm of rain a year against 1,491 mm of evaporative demand, 74 days above 35 °C, and bare soil for 155 days of every year.

Agriverto turns that record into a decision. It takes any field from its coordinates, reads NASA POWER climate data, MODIS vegetation and SMAP soil moisture, adds local soil properties and crop characteristics, and compares the farmer’s current rotation against four alternatives. The farmer sets what matters to them — saving water, building soil, adding income — and sees which rotation fits, in real units: millimetres of irrigation, days of bare soil, kilograms of nitrogen, percent of yield at risk in a dry year.

It is built to be checked, not believed. Every number traces to a dataset or a published FAO coefficient, and where the data cannot answer, the tool says so. It recommends; the farmer and their agronomist decide.
details:
What it does

Agriverto compares crop rotations for any field on Earth. The farmer picks a field — one of five presets or any point on a map — enters the crops they grow in order, and sets six priorities: saving water, soil organic matter, nitrogen fixing, erosion reduction, forage value, and income. The app then shows two things. First, what the land is actually like: rainfall against evapotranspiration month by month, frost dates, hot days, the satellite’s view of how green the field gets through the year, and when the ground sits bare. Second, five rotations compared side by side, the farmer’s own always included, each with the irrigation it needs, the bare days it leaves, the nitrogen it fixes, and the yield at risk if water runs short. Sliders test every recommendation under less rain, more heat, or less irrigation water.

How it works

For any coordinates, Agriverto pulls about 25 years of daily NASA POWER weather and computes growing degree days, frost dates, heat-stress days, reference evapotranspiration by the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method, and the monthly water balance. MODIS NDVI gives the observed growth curve and bare-soil periods; SMAP gives soil moisture where its quality flags allow; ISRIC SoilGrids gives soil texture, organic carbon and pH. A crop knowledge base holds about 20 crops with their water needs, temperature limits, season lengths, nitrogen fixing, root depth and pest families, using FAO-56 crop coefficients and FAO-33 yield response factors. Rotations are generated by agronomic rules — insert a legume, fill a bare window with a cover crop, swap a thirsty crop for a drought-tolerant one — checked for calendar feasibility, then scored against every historical year, so results come with a range across dry, normal and wet years rather than a single number.

Benefits and intended impact

NASA’s agricultural data is free and global, but it arrives as satellite products rather than as a planting decision. Agriverto closes that gap for one decision, in the farmer’s own language. For the Fergana field, it finds winter wheat followed by mung bean: a fit of 72 against 17 for wheat and cotton, bare soil cut from 155 days to 55, at the cost of 18% more irrigation water. Less bare soil means less erosion and evaporation; a legume adds nitrogen the next crop can use. The tool works for any coordinates, so it is not limited to the regions we tested.

What makes it creative

Two things. First, it treats uncertainty as content rather than something to hide. The satellite cannot see this field through snow and cloud for about 90 days a year, so the app says so on screen instead of filling the gap. Reanalysis temperature runs hot over irrigated land, so the app says the hot-day count is likely overstated. Second, the satellite data independently supports the recommendation: this field turns green again after every wheat harvest in all seven years since 2019, which suggests farmers already plant a second crop in that gap — and Agriverto reaches the same answer from climate and crop science alone.

Tools

Python 3.12, Streamlit, pandas, numpy, plotly, folium and Leaflet. NASA GIBS tile layers for the map overlays. 576 automated tests, including the FAO-56 worked example for the evapotranspiration calculation. Deployed on an Oracle Cloud virtual machine behind nginx with a Let’s Encrypt certificate, and it ships with cached data so it runs without a network connection.

What we considered

That a recommendation must be checkable: every number traces to a dataset or a published coefficient, and estimated values are flagged as approximate. That a farmer may not be free to change crops, so the app states that it does not know about contracts or obligations. That the tool should support rather than replace local expertise, which it says on every screen. And that it had to work in Uzbek, not only English.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources) The backbone of the project. About 25 years of daily temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind, solar radiation and soil wetness at ~50 km resolution, for any coordinates. Every climate indicator is computed from it: growing degree days, frost dates, heat-stress days, FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration, the monthly water balance, and the dry/normal/wet year classification.

MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day L3 Global 250m (MOD13Q1.061) The observed crop growth curve and bare-soil periods for each field, 2019–2026, with per-pixel quality filtering. This is what shows the field turning green again after every wheat harvest. Didan, K. (2021). NASA Land Processes DAAC.

SMAP Enhanced L3 Radiometer Global and Polar Grid Daily 9 km EASE-Grid Soil Moisture, Version 6 (SPL3SMP_E) Surface soil moisture. Usable at our Kansas and Karakalpakstan fields; rejected by its own quality flags at Fergana, which the app reports rather than hides. O’Neill, P., Chan, S., Njoku, E., Jackson, T., Bindlish, R., Chaubell, J., & Colliander, A. (2023). NASA NSIDC DAAC.

NASA Worldview / GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services) Four switchable map layers with their real observation dates and legends: MODIS vegetation index, GPM IMERG precipitation rate, MODIS land surface temperature, and SMAP Level-4 surface soil moisture. Used as regional context on the map, not in the scoring.

AppEEARS (Application for Extracting and Exploring Analysis Ready Samples) NASA’s extraction service, used to sample MODIS and SMAP at our exact field coordinates with their quality layers. AppEEARS Team (2026), Ver. 3.137, NASA LP DAAC
NASA Earthdata Login Authentication and data access for the above.
